title: Ultraviolet Radiation: Evidence and Safety
objective: Separate UV-A, UV-B, and UV-C exposure, evaluate cannabis claims against dose-defined evidence, and prioritize worker controls.

terms.definition: Ultraviolet radiation from 315 to 400 nm under the convention used here.
Ultraviolet radiation from 280 to 315 nm under the convention used here.
Ultraviolet radiation from 100 to 280 nm, including germicidal wavelengths; not a routine photosynthetic-light treatment.
Time-integrated irradiance or photon exposure within a defined wavelength band and geometry.

coreScience: Ultraviolet bands differ in photon energy, plant response, material effects, and human hazard. A statement that a crop received 'UV' is scientifically inadequate without wavelength distribution, irradiance or photon flux, duration, distance, orientation, timing, and cumulative dose.

Cannabis claims that UV reliably increases cannabinoids are not supported as a universal rule. In a controlled study of one high-THC cultivar, the evaluated UV-A and UV-A plus UV-B treatments did not increase yield or cannabinoid content. A result from one cultivar and dose does not prove that all UV treatments are ineffective, but it directly rejects certainty.

UV can injure eyes and skin and degrade plastics, cables, sensors, and biological tissues. NIOSH-supported work in cannabis facilities recommends choosing low-UV-emitting lamps and using engineering controls, including interlocks for germicidal lamps. Access control, shielding, signage, training, exposure assessment, and verified shutdown states take priority over speculative crop benefit.
cultivationRelevance: A UV trial requires an approved safety review, exposure measurement with a suitable instrument, a no-exposure work procedure, and a defined scientific hypothesis.
UV-C used for disinfection is a separate hazard-controlled process and should not be improvised as a crop-lighting channel or operated in occupied space.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Lamp model, spectral emission, band, peak wavelength, ageing, warm-up, distance, orientation, and shielding.
Irradiance or photon flux by band, dose, duration, schedule, measurement instrument, and uncertainty.
Risk assessment, interlocks, access state, signage, training, PPE basis, exposure survey, and incident log.
Cultivar, stage, control treatment, background PPFD/DLI, symptoms, yield, and laboratory outcomes.
Fixture, sensor, plastic, hose, cable, and surface inspection plus replacement interval.

misconceptions: UV always boosts potency: Controlled cannabis evidence is mixed and treatment-specific; universal claims are unsupported.
UV-A is harmless: Risk depends on wavelength and dose; eye, skin, and material exposure still require assessment.
PPE makes an open UV system acceptable: Engineering controls and preventing exposure are preferred before reliance on personal protection.
evidenceLimits: UV studies use different spectra, radiometric units, doses, cultivars, stages, and background light. Results cannot be generalized without matching those conditions and independently validating safety.
